source: བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་རྣམས་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་འཇུག་པར་མི་འགྱུར་བ་ནས་ཇི་སྲིད་གལ་ཏེ་ཆོས་མེད་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་ན་དེ་ཉིད་དེ་དག་གི་བདག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་བྱ་བས་ནི་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཡང་དག་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ལོག་པར་འཛིན་པ་ལྔའི་གཉེན་པོར་ཏེ། ལོག་པར་འཛིན་པ་ལྔ་པོ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེ་ན། གཞན་མུ་སྟེགས་བྱེད་དག་ཆོས་འདི་ལ་དང་། སོ་སོའི་སྐྱེ་བོ་དང་། ཉན་ཐོས་དང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་ཅན་དང་། འཇིག་རྟེན་པ་ཐུན་མོང་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་སུ་ལྟུང་བ་རྣམས་སམ། འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་པར་ལྟུང་བ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་སྟེ། དང་པོ་ནི་བདག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་ལ། གཉིས་པ་ནི་ཆོས་སུ་འདུ་ཤེས་ཤིང་། གསུམ་པ་ནི་ཆོས་མ་ཡིན་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་སྟེ། ཆོས་ལ་དངོས་པོར་འདུ་ཤེས་པས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པ་ནི་འདིར་ཆོས་མ་ཡིན་པར་འདོད་དོ། །བཞི་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་པ་དང་། ལྔ་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་པ་སྟེ།བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་རྣམས་ནི་འདི་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་ལྡན་པ་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ནས་ཇི་སྲིད་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་ཉེ་བར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །
translation: The statement "those bodhisattvas do not engage in the perception of a sentient being, up to the point that if they were to engage in the perception of the non-existence of phenomena, that very thing would become their grasping at a self" indicates their correct perception. This is the antidote to five types of erroneous grasping. What are these five types of erroneous grasping? They are the perceptions of others—such as tīrthikas, ordinary beings, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas who possess pride, and those who fall into the perception of worldly commonality—or those who fall into the perception of non-perception. The first involves engaging in the perception of a self; the second involves the perception of phenomena; the third involves the perception of non-phenomena, for because they perceive phenomena as substantial, the non-existence of the substantiality of phenomena is here considered to be "non-phenomena." The fourth is engaging in the perception of [a self], and the fifth is the perception of non-perception. Those bodhisattvas do not engage in the perception of any of these. Therefore, it is taught that "they will possess ethical conduct," up to the point that "they will possess an immeasurable mass of merit."

heading: གཟུགས་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པ།
translation: Because it is stated, "For what reason?", it is because whatever erroneous grasping occurs is the engaging in the perception of phenomena and the perception of non-phenomena. That which is the non-engagement of the perception of selflessness and so forth is also a perception of a self and so forth; because those latent tendencies have not been abandoned, this very thing becomes grasping at a self. Therefore, if those bodhisattvas engage in the perception of phenomena, that very thing becomes their grasping at a self. By stating "if they engage in the perception of non-phenomena," it is taught that the remaining ones also engage in the perception of a self and so forth.

[2-24] translation already produced for this document:
The statement "those bodhisattvas do not engage in the perception of a sentient being, up to the point that if they were to engage in the perception of the non-existence of phenomena, that very thing would become their grasping at a self" indicates their correct perception. This is the antidote to five types of erroneous grasping. What are these five types of erroneous grasping? They are the perceptions of others—such as tīrthikas, ordinary beings, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas who possess pride, and those who fall into the perception of worldly commonality—or those who fall into the perception of non-perception. The first involves engaging in the perception of a self; the second involves the perception of phenomena; the third involves the perception of non-phenomena, for because they perceive phenomena as substantial, the non-existence of the substantiality of phenomena is here considered to be "non-phenomena." The fourth is engaging in the perception of [a self], and the fifth is the perception of non-perception. Those bodhisattvas do not engage in the perception of any of these. Therefore, it is taught that "they will possess ethical conduct," up to the point that "they will possess an immeasurable mass of merit."

heading: གཟུགས་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པ།
translation: Even if the word "itself" is not stated, it means that this very thing becomes their grasping at a self. In this regard, the grasping that determines [something] as one's own continuum is to be understood as the perception of a self, and the grasping at the existence of what is "mine" is the perception of a sentient being. The grasping at a self as enduring for as long as life lasts is the perception of a life force. The grasping at going into the realms of rebirth again and again is the perception of a person. It is said that for those, one should generate the correct perception. Regarding the words of the sūtra that will be explained, the incorrect perception of the meaning being lost is shown to be the adverse factor, whereas by merely stating the cause, the Dharmakāya that is taught is fully revealed.

[2-25] translation already produced for this document:
Because it is stated, "For what reason?", it is because whatever erroneous grasping occurs is the engaging in the perception of phenomena and the perception of non-phenomena. That which is the non-engagement of the perception of selflessness and so forth is also a perception of a self and so forth; because those latent tendencies have not been abandoned, this very thing becomes grasping at a self. Therefore, if those bodhisattvas engage in the perception of phenomena, that very thing becomes their grasping at a self. By stating "if they engage in the perception of non-phenomena," it is taught that the remaining ones also engage in the perception of a self and so forth.

heading: བསྟན་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: The statement "generate the correct perception" indicates the aspiration and prayer for generating that [perception]. The statement "their grasping at a self will not occur" sets forth the ultimate meaning in detail. Furthermore, the statement "Subhūti, one should not grasp at a dharma, nor at what is not a dharma" indicates the cutting off of the distraction of one who has entered into meditative equipoise; the meaning is that at that time, both grasping at what is not a dharma and grasping at what is not "not a dharma" are conceptualizations regarding the selflessness of phenomena. That is the Dharmakāya that is taught. Therefore, the Tathāgata spoke this for the sake of sentient beings.

heading: བསྟན་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: For those who understand the discourse on the Dharma as being like a raft, even the Dharma is to be abandoned; thus, it is taught that before generating the correct perception, what is not a dharma—these things—are taught. heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།

Is there any dharma that the Tathāgata has taught as unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?" By this, he indicates that to grasp at an awakening that is to be realized, based on the degeneration of the meaning, is a discordant factor; it is said that by teaching the Dharma, one grasps at that as perfect awakening. Therefore, he said, "Is there any dharma that has been taught?"—namely, what is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. By merely expressing the cause, the Dharmakāya of realization is taught. By saying "No," the Elder Subhūti expressed the Buddha’s intention, indicating an aspiration and prayer that is free from grasping at awakening in a conventional sense; he intended that, in terms of the discourse, both of these exist. The Blessed One’s statement indicates that, in that sense, neither of these exists.

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: "Not to be grasped and not to be expressed; it is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma"—by this, he establishes the ultimate, for the sake of realizing the taught dharma, which is awakening. He establishes the ultimate by taking the nature of phenomena as the basis; in this context, "not to be grasped" means it cannot be listened to. "Not to be expressed" means there is no dharma that is the very thing taught, and because of the selflessness of phenomena, there is also no non-dharma in terms of the nature of the imagined.

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: "Why is this?" The statement "Noble beings are distinguished by the unconditioned" means that they do not conceptualize in terms of conditioned phenomena; by this, the bodhisattva who is a learner is distinguished. "Unborn" means that although it exists, it is unconditioned, and because the transformation of the Tathāgata's state is distinguished by the purity of suchness, by this, the Tathāgata who is a non-learner is distinguished. In this context, the first meaning of "unconditioned" indicates entering into meditative equipoise, and it also indicates the subduing of distraction therein. The second meaning indicates the unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment, which has the meaning of the perfection of wisdom. From this, one should understand that all higher supports are distinguished by the unconditioned, as this is said with the noble beings in mind. Because the unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment is taught here without having previously spoken of being distinguished by the unconditioned, the unconditioned is attained by way of its meaning. If one asks what is being fully taught regarding the support of the dharmakāya that realizes the nature of merit, it is because the dharmakāya that is realized from the Tathāgatas—who have a nature endowed with merit—arises from the dharmakāya that is taught for the time being. That is also how the teaching of the four-line verse is to be understood for the time being. The source of great merit is, in the first instance, this dharmakāya that is realized by the Tathāgatas, which is the nature of merit.

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Therefore, Subhūti, the statement "Buddha-dharmas, Buddha-dharmas" is taught as "the absence of those Buddha-dharmas." In this regard, this is to be understood for the time being as the cause for the arising of much merit; however, by the falling away of the meaning, it is fully taught that the opposing side of merit arises abundantly. By merely expressing the cause called "merit," the Dharmakāya, which is the nature of merit, is fully taught. By the very teaching of supreme merit, one also demonstrates the aspiration for it: "Bhagavān, that very mass of merit is a non-mass, and therefore the Tathāgata has spoken of it as a 'mass of merit'."

heading: རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: "Subhūti, the statement 'Buddha-dharmas, Buddha-dharmas' is taught as 'the absence of those Buddha-dharmas,' and therefore they are called 'Buddha-dharmas.' By this, the mass of merit that was spoken of is also addressed; for whoever fully grasps the Buddha-dharmas, the Dharmakāya, which is the nature of merit, is established in the ultimate sense, based on the fact that it belongs to those Tathāgatas. This is a further teaching to cut off the distraction of one who has entered into meditative equipoise, following the instruction that 'noble beings are distinguished by the unconditioned.' 'Bhagavān, it is much; Sugata, it is much'—the utterance of these two phrases indicates that it is grasped as a self-nature, and thus it points to a self-nature that is grasped as a self; it is taught as taking hold of what is grasped as superior, which is the meaning of the statement 'it should be taught by words and letters.' 'Immeasurable' means it is not an object of analogy, and 'countless' means it is vast. This is the basis of aspiration. The basis of being free from obstacles should be understood as the antidote to the twelve obstacles. What are the twelve obstacles? They are: having manifest pride; even if one is without manifest pride, having little learning; even if one has much learning, practicing only minor mental engagement; even if one’s mental engagement is not minor, abandoning sentient beings; even if one does not abandon them, being attached to external treatises; even if one does not engage in those, being unskilled in suppressing the signs of illusions; even if one is skilled in that, not accumulating the collection of merit; even if one accumulates the collection of merit, being overcome by laziness and tasting the flavor of the happiness of honor and respect; even if one does not taste that flavor, being unable to endure suffering; even if one can endure suffering, not accumulating the collection of wisdom; and even if one accumulates the collection of wisdom, holding to a self, or even if one does not hold to a self, being devoid of oral instructions.

Therefore, Subhūti, the statement "Buddha-dharmas, Buddha-dharmas" is taught as "the absence of those Buddha-dharmas." In this regard, this is to be understood for the time being as the cause for the arising of much merit; however, by the falling away of the meaning, it is fully taught that the opposing side of merit arises abundantly. By merely expressing the cause called "merit," the Dharmakāya, which is the nature of merit, is fully taught. By the very teaching of supreme merit, one also demonstrates the aspiration for it: "Bhagavān, that very mass of merit is a non-mass, and therefore the Tathāgata has spoken of it as a 'mass of merit'."

heading: བསྒོམ་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་རྟོགས་པ་ལ་མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་མེད་པ།

heading: སངས་རྒྱས་འབྱུང་བ་མཉེས་པར་བྱེད་པ།
translation: In order to emphasize the state of being free from having heard little, the Tathāgata asked, "Was there any dharma that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara obtained?" The failure of meaning is due to the application of the practice to discordant factors and the like.

Regarding that, the size of the body of the asura-king Rāhu is equal to Mount Meru, and even that is to be viewed as temporarily lacking a body; what need is there to mention others?

[2-42] translation already produced for this document:
In order to emphasize the state of being free from the meditation of minor mental engagement with objects, it is stated at length: "Subhūti, if any bodhisattva were to say, 'I shall accomplish the arrays of the buddha-fields'..." When one mentally engages with the arrays of the fields, one tastes the flavor of that which is based on the conceptualization of form and the like.

[2-43] source:
དེ་ཡོངས་སུ་སྤང་བའི་དོན་དུ་རབ་འབྱོར་དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་འདི་ལྟར་མི་གནས་པར་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱའོ། །
[2-43] translation already produced for this document:
For the purpose of completely abandoning that, [it is said]: "Subhūti, therefore, a bodhisattva should give rise to the mind of awakening in this way, by not dwelling."

[2-44] source:
ཅི་ལ་ཡང་མི་གནས་པར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདི་རྒྱས་པར་གསུངས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[2-44] translation already produced for this document:
This is what is explained at length by the words, "by not dwelling in anything at all."

heading: སེམས་ཅན་ཡོངས་སུ་སྨིན་པར་བྱེད་པ།
translation: The statement "The Tathāgata has spoken of the absence of entities" indicates the selflessness of phenomena as suchness. To say "there are no entities" is to point completely to the suchness that is non-arisen and unconditioned. This is to point completely to the selflessness of phenomena in terms of their intrinsic nature and their specific characteristics.

heading: ཕྱི་རོལ་གྱི་བསྟན་བཅོས་སྙིང་པོ་མེད་པ་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་པས་དབེན་པ།
translation: In order to emphasize the state of being free from attachment to the essence-less treatises of outsiders, it is stated at length: "Subhūti, what do you think? As many as are the grains of sand in the river Ganges..." Here, four causes are used to point completely to the excellence of this Dharma: the accumulation of merit, being honored by many such as gods, the cause of performing hardships, and being contemplated and accompanied by the Tathāgata and others.

heading: ཕྱི་རོལ་གྱི་བསྟན་བཅོས་སྙིང་པོ་མེད་པ་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་པས་དབེན་པ།

heading: ཕྱི་རོལ་གྱི་བསྟན་བཅོས་སྙིང་པོ་མེད་པ་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་པས་དབེན་པ།
translation: The statement "The Teacher also abides in that place, and other places of the Guru also abide" refers to being contemplated and accompanied by the Tathāgata and others. Regarding this, it is said "to be taught by way of what has been spoken and what will be spoken, and by way of the Teacher." By thoroughly pointing out the excellence of this Dharma as an antidote to attachment to the essence-less treatises of outsiders, one should not become attached to this very Dharma as if it were merely the literal words; rather, it serves as an antidote to the future faults of those [treatises].

heading: ཕྱི་རོལ་གྱི་བསྟན་བཅོས་སྙིང་པོ་མེད་པ་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་པས་དབེན་པ།
translation: The statement "That which the Tathāgata has spoken as the prajñāpāramitā is not a pāramitā" means that just as the prajñāpāramitā is not a pāramitā, in the same way, the Tathāgata has not taught any Dharma at all; this is the meaning being thoroughly pointed out. It is said "what the Tathāgata has spoken as Dharma," and this discourse on Dharma thoroughly points out the ultimate reality through its own and general characteristics.

translation: Because those who are unskilled in suppressing the signs of images are in need of being led away from them, it is explained at length: "Subhūti, as for the number of atoms of earth in the great trichiliocosm world system..." This is because Bodhisattvas who contemplate great objects will extensively cultivate the mental engagement of focusing on world systems; therefore, the great trichiliocosm world system is mentioned.

In this regard, the purpose of suppressing the signs of the images is fully taught, but it is not a method for making them subtle.

heading: དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་མཆོད་ཅིང་བསྙེན་བཀུར་བ།

heading: དུབ་པའི་ཡོངས་སུ་གདུང་བ་ལ་བརྩོན་པ་བཟློག་ནས་མ་བརྩམས་པའི་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་དབེན་པ།
translation: With regard to those who are devoid of having tasted the bliss of laziness, gain, and honor, it is stated at length: "Subhūti, what if a man or woman were to give away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges?" What is taught by this? It is that while the merit from giving away bodies for a time is indeed that much, one should not be interrupted by the laziness that relies upon a single body for as long as one exists.

translation: Why does the Elder Subhūti shed tears? It is stated: "Since I have attained wisdom, I have not heard such a discourse on the Dharma." Although I have heard that giving away a great many bodies results in great and supreme merit, this is not teaching that merit is supreme here; rather, having heard that merit becomes supreme in that way, one initiates diligence and develops a perception of the Dharma just as it is.

heading: དུབ་པའི་ཡོངས་སུ་གདུང་བ་ལ་བརྩོན་པ་བཟློག་ནས་མ་བརྩམས་པའི་རྙེད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟིས་དབེན་པ།
translation: Based on the state of being free from non-exertion, it is explained in detail that "in this regard, one will not be afraid when the words of the sūtra are explained." Fear is the failure to initiate diligence. The Bhagavat has taught that for the Śrāvaka vehicle, there is the emptiness of phenomena alone, whereas for the Mahāyāna, it is taught that neither exists by way of an imputed nature. Upon hearing this, one becomes afraid when hearing that phenomena do not exist, and one becomes terrified when hearing that emptiness is without substantiality; and when one contemplates that because both are without substantiality, one is unable to apply or engage in them, one becomes completely terrified. Furthermore, one should understand this as a series of synonyms based on the three types of lack of intrinsic nature: the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics, and the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of the ultimate.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་བཟོད་པ།
translation: In terms of being free from the inability to endure suffering, the Tathāgata has further spoken at length, "Subhūti, the Tathāgata’s kṣānti-pāramitā." Regarding this, by what signs can one know that kṣānti which has been spoken of? What is the nature of kṣānti? What is the cause and the antidote of kṣānti? I shall state it: the teaching that kṣānti is just as it is through the individual realization of the selflessness of phenomena is what is meant by the statement, "That which is the Tathāgata’s kṣānti-pāramitā is itself not a pāramitā." By what sign should one recognize kṣānti? If, while being harmed, one does not have the perception of a malicious mind arising from the basis of the perception of a self and so forth, that is it. One does not perceive this as being the kṣānti-pāramitā, nor does one perceive it as not being a pāramitā; thus, its nature is taught.

Why is that? Regarding the statement, "Subhūti, this supreme prajñāpāramitā has been spoken by the Tathāgata," what is the meaning? It establishes the second basis of shame, meaning that because this teaching is paramount, one should be conscientious. In this regard, the other pāramitās are pāramitās only because of this paramount nature.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་བཟོད་པ།
translation: It is stated at length, "When the King of Kalinga severed my limbs and appendages, at that time I had no perception of a self." Regarding this, how is it that one endures in such a manner? It is to fully demonstrate how one endures intense suffering and also endures continuous suffering, which is why it is stated, "When the King of Kalinga severed my limbs and appendages."

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་བཟོད་པ།
translation: Regarding that, the statement, "Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should generate the mind for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by completely abandoning all perceptions," is a teaching on the antidote to the cause of not enduring the suffering of saṃsāra. There are three types of generating the mind for enlightenment: it is the unwillingness to generate it due to the perception of suffering; therefore, it is stated at length, "by completely abandoning all perceptions." Here, there are three types: the perception of suffering, all perceptions of desiring to dwell in form and so forth, and the mind not generating enlightenment because it is completely exhausted by these sufferings of saṃsāra.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་བཟོད་པ།
translation: Likewise, the statement, "One should not abide in phenomena, nor should one abide in non-phenomena," means that one should not abide in phenomena, nor should one abide in the selflessness of phenomena. The state of not abiding in them is explained at length as follows: because that which is "abiding" is itself non-abiding, in order to refute the conceptualization of an intrinsic nature that corresponds literally to the words used here.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་བཟོད་པ།
translation: Furthermore, the statement, "A bodhisattva should completely give away gifts for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings," and the explanation at length, "Whatever perception of sentient beings there is, that itself is also a non-perception," fully demonstrate the antidote to the cause of not enduring the suffering of being harmed by sentient beings; it is said that one gives away everything for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings. Since those sentient beings—to whom one is attached, thinking, "I am the agent and this is the action"—do not exist, from what cause could there be a perception of sentient beings that would produce weariness toward the wrong practices of sentient beings? Thus, it also fully demonstrates the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་བཟོད་པ།
translation: Subhūti, what is being taught by the extensive statement, "The Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth"? It means that one should also endure through having genuine faith in the Tathāgata. In this regard, "one who speaks the truth" is stated in terms of the characteristics of conventional truth. "One who speaks the truth" is stated in terms of the characteristics of the thoroughly afflicted and the completely purified. "This" refers to the truth of the practice, which is to say, "one should be thoroughly afflicted and one should be completely purified."

Furthermore, the statement, "A bodhisattva should completely give away gifts for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings," and the explanation at length, "Whatever perception of sentient beings there is, that itself is also a non-perception," fully demonstrate the antidote to the cause of not enduring the suffering of being harmed by sentient beings; it is said that one gives away everything for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings. Since those sentient beings—to whom one is attached, thinking, "I am the agent and this is the action"—do not exist, from what cause could there be a perception of sentient beings that would produce weariness toward the wrong practices of sentient beings? Thus, it also fully demonstrates the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena.

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་བཟོད་པ།
translation: It is in terms of the characteristics of ultimate truth that the Tathāgata is spoken of as "suchness." It is in terms of the characteristics of the thoroughly afflicted and the completely purified that the Tathāgata is spoken of as "suchness" and as "one who speaks the truth." Here, "truth" refers to the fact that, in order to completely abandon the clinging to a literal essence, the Tathāgata has stated that for any phenomenon that he has fully awakened to or taught, there is neither truth nor falsehood. There is no truth because it is devoid of a literal essence; there is no falsehood because it exists as a non-literal essence.

Subhūti, what is being taught by the extensive statement, "The Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth"? It means that one should also endure through having genuine faith in the Tathāgata. In this regard, "one who speaks the truth" is stated in terms of the characteristics of conventional truth. "One who speaks the truth" is stated in terms of the characteristics of the thoroughly afflicted and the completely purified. "This" refers to the truth of the practice, which is to say, "one should be thoroughly afflicted and one should be completely purified."

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་བཟོད་པ།
translation: Subhūti, the extensive statement, "It is like a person who has entered the darkness," fully demonstrates the antidote to the cause of not enduring the suffering of lacking material resources. Whoever gives gifts for the sake of material resources is giving gifts while falling into the perception of entities, and that falling is for the sake of desiring happiness and being free from suffering.

རབ་འབྱོར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ནི་ཡང་དག་པར་གསུང་པ་ཞེས་རྒྱས་པས་ཅི་ཞིག་སྟོན་ཞེ་ན། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཡིད་ཆེས་པས་ཀྱང་བཟོད་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལ་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཀྱི་བདེན་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས་ཡང་དག་པར་གསུང་པའོ། །དེ་སྒྲུབ་པ་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་རྣམ་པར་བྱང་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས་བདེན་པ་གསུང་པའོ། །འདི་ནི་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་རྣམ་པར་བྱང་བར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བདེན་པའི་སྒྲུབ་པའོ། །
[2-75] translation already produced for this document:
Subhūti, what is being taught by the extensive statement, "The Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth"? It means that one should also endure through having genuine faith in the Tathāgata. In this regard, "one who speaks the truth" is stated in terms of the characteristics of conventional truth. "One who speaks the truth" is stated in terms of the characteristics of the thoroughly afflicted and the completely purified. "This" refers to the truth of the practice, which is to say, "one should be thoroughly afflicted and one should be completely purified."

heading: སྡུག་བསྔལ་བཟོད་པ།
translation: Feelings do not generate a definitive renunciation; just as one who has entered the darkness thinks, "How can I proceed?" and therefore delights in the pleasure of desire, the one who gives gifts without falling into the perception of entities is like a person with sight at daybreak, when the sun has risen and diverse forms are seen, who looks, thinking, "How shall I proceed?" That person, having passed the night of ignorance and with the sun of wisdom having risen, generates the vision of diverse knowable objects exactly as they are. Otherwise, one would not delight in the pleasure of desire, for there is a definitive renunciation from the feelings of pleasure and pain of desire.

[2-76] translation already produced for this document:
It is in terms of the characteristics of ultimate truth that the Tathāgata is spoken of as "suchness." It is in terms of the characteristics of the thoroughly afflicted and the completely purified that the Tathāgata is spoken of as "suchness" and as "one who speaks the truth." Here, "truth" refers to the fact that, in order to completely abandon the clinging to a literal essence, the Tathāgata has stated that for any phenomenon that he has fully awakened to or taught, there is neither truth nor falsehood. There is no truth because it is devoid of a literal essence; there is no falsehood because it exists as a non-literal essence.

[2-77] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ་དཔེར་ན། མི་ཞིག་མུན་པར་ཞུགས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་རྒྱས་པས་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་མ་ཚང་བའི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལ་མི་བཟོད་པའི་རྒྱུའི་གཉེན་པོ་ཡོངས་སུ་སྟོན་ཏེ། སུ་ཞིག་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་ཀྱི་དོན་དུ་སྦྱིན་པ་གཏོང་བ་དེ་ནི་དངོས་པོར་ལྟུང་བས་སྦྱིན་པ་གཏོང་བ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་ལྟུང་བ་ནི་བདེ་བ་འདོད་ཅིང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་མེད་པའི་ཆེད་དུའོ། །
[2-77] translation already produced for this document:
Subhūti, the extensive statement, "It is like a person who has entered the darkness," fully demonstrates the antidote to the cause of not enduring the suffering of lacking material resources. Whoever gives gifts for the sake of material resources is giving gifts while falling into the perception of entities, and that falling is for the sake of desiring happiness and being free from suffering.

heading: ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གྱི་རོ་མྱང་བས་དབེན་པ།
translation: In order to address the lack of the accumulation of wisdom, it is said, "Subhūti, any son or daughter of good family who takes up this discourse on the Dharma," and so forth. Here, for the sake of those who are devoid of tasting the flavor of samādhi, five distinct qualities of what is called the yoga of Dharma are demonstrated: being kept in mind and accompanied by the Tathāgata, the complete acquisition of merit, praise for practicing the Dharma, being honored by gods and others, and the exhaustion of negative deeds. What is meant by being kept in mind and accompanied by the Tathāgata? It is what was said: "The Tathāgata knows them; the Tathāgata beholds them."

Whoever gives gifts for the sake of material resources is giving gifts while falling into the perception of entities, and that falling is for the sake of desiring happiness and being free from suffering.

[2-78] source:
ཚོར་བས་ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་བ་སྐྱེད་པར་མི་བྱེད་དེ། ཇི་ལྟར་མུན་པར་ཞུགས་པ་ཅི་ནས་བདག་གིས་འགྲོ་བར་བྱའོ་སྙམ་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར་འདོད་པའི་བདེ་བ་ཉིད་ལ་མངོན་པར་དགའ་ཞིང་གང་དངོས་པོར་མ་ལྷུང་བས་སྦྱིན་པ་བྱིན་པ་དེ་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་མིག་དང་ལྡན་པའི་མི་ནམ་ལངས་ཏེ་ཉི་མ་ཤར་ནས་གཟུགས་སྣ་ཚོགས་པ་མཐོང་བ་གང་ལས་བདག་གིས་འགྲོ་བར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་དེ་ལྟར་བལྟའོ། །དེ་ནི་མ་རིག་པའི་མཚན་མོ་འདས་ཤིང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཉི་མ་ཤར་བ་ན་རྣམ་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་པའི་ཤེས་བྱ་ཡང་དག་པ་ཇི་ལྟ་བཞིན་དུ་མཐོང་བ་སྐྱེད་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །གཞན་དུ་འདོད་པའི་བདེ་བ་དང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱིས་ཚོར་བ་ལས་ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་བ་དེའི་ཕྱིར་འདོད་པའི་བདེ་བ་ལ་མངོན་པར་དགའ་བ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[2-78] translation already produced for this document:
Feelings do not generate a definitive renunciation; just as one who has entered the darkness thinks, "How can I proceed?" and therefore delights in the pleasure of desire, the one who gives gifts without falling into the perception of entities is like a person with sight at daybreak, when the sun has risen and diverse forms are seen, who looks, thinking, "How shall I proceed?" That person, having passed the night of ignorance and with the sun of wisdom having risen, generates the vision of diverse knowable objects exactly as they are. Otherwise, one would not delight in the pleasure of desire, for there is a definitive renunciation from the feelings of pleasure and pain of desire.

heading: ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གྱི་རོ་མྱང་བས་དབེན་པ།
source: དེ་ལ་ལེན་པ་དང་། ཀློག་པ་དང་། འཛིན་པ་དང་། མི་བརྗེད་པར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། སྨྲ་བར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། ཀུན་ཆུབ་པར་བྱེད་པ་ཞེས་གང་གསུངས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འཛིན་པའི་གཟུངས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ་ལེན་པར་འདོད་པ་དང་། ཀློག་པ་དང་འཛིན་པར་འདོད་པ་དང་ཀུན་ཆུབ་པར་བྱེད་པའོ། །ཡང་སྨྲ་བར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། ཀློག་པར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། ཀུན་ཆུབ་པར་བྱེད་པ་ཞེས་དོན་འཛིན་པར་བྱེད་པའོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་བསོད་ནམས་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་ཞེ་ན། སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ནི་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་བསྐྱེད་དོ་ཞེས་གང་གསུངས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །མི་བརྗེད་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་ཀྱང་རྒྱས་པར་རོ། །
translation: Regarding that, it is what was said: "taking up, reading, retaining, not forgetting, speaking, and mastering." This refers to taking up the cause of the dhāraṇī of retention, and the desire to read, retain, and master. Furthermore, "speaking, reading, and mastering" refers to retaining the meaning. If you ask how merit is completely acquired, it is what was said: "All those sentient beings will generate an immeasurable heap of merit." It is also explained at length that they will not forget.

Regarding that, it is what was said: "taking up, reading, retaining, not forgetting, speaking, and mastering." This refers to taking up the cause of the dhāraṇī of retention, and the desire to read, retain, and master. Furthermore, "speaking, reading, and mastering" refers to retaining the meaning. If you ask how merit is completely acquired, it is what was said: "All those sentient beings will generate an immeasurable heap of merit." It is also explained at length that they will not forget.

heading: ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གྱི་རོ་མྱང་བས་དབེན་པ།
translation: In order to fully demonstrate the many ways in which they are completely worn away, it is stated that they will be "extremely worn away," that the awakening of a Buddha will also be attained, and that obscurations and negative deeds will be completely exhausted. Therefore, it is also said that, furthermore, they will emerge from falling [into lower realms], and that extremely numerous, immeasurable, and innumerable merits will arise. It should be understood that this is an explanation of "immeasurable" and "innumerable," because it is also the case that extreme suffering will arise and that a great multitude will arise.

heading: ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གྱི་རོ་མྱང་བས་དབེན་པ།
translation: Regarding that, the statement "Subhūti, I cognize the immeasurable and even more immeasurable eons," and so forth, as explained at length, indicates that which is supreme. This is the arising of the heap of merit of this [sūtra], and that heap of merit is supreme and surpasses all others. Regarding that, it should be understood that for as long as the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara existed, it was for immeasurable eons; the statement that "by that, one has pleased [the Buddhas] in ways that are even more immeasurable" is a summary. "Not having produced a thought" means being without pride.

heading: ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གྱི་རོ་མྱང་བས་དབེན་པ།

Regarding that, it should be understood that the "myo myo po" (the confused state) is the cause, and the "disturbed mind" is the result.

Regarding that, it means making offerings with flowers, incense, parasols, victory banners, flags, and so forth, as well as bowing down, paying homage, circumambulating, offering alms, and [making it a place] that becomes a stūpa. What is meant by the exhaustion of negative deeds? It is that these [negative deeds] will be completely worn away.

Regarding that, the statement "Subhūti, I cognize the immeasurable and even more immeasurable eons," and so forth, as explained at length, indicates that which is supreme. This is the arising of the heap of merit of this [sūtra], and that heap of merit is supreme and surpasses all others. Regarding that, it should be understood that for as long as the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara existed, it was for immeasurable eons; the statement that "by that, one has pleased [the Buddhas] in ways that are even more immeasurable" is a summary. "Not having produced a thought" means being without pride.

Furthermore, the statement "Subhūti, if I were to describe the heap of merit of those sons or daughters of noble family," and so forth, as explained at length, indicates a great multitude. Regarding that, it should be understood that the "myo myo po" (the confused state) is the cause, and the "disturbed mind" is the result.

heading: མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་དུས་སུ་བདག་གོ་སྙམ་དུ་འཛིན་པས་དབེན་པ།
translation: The statement "How," and so forth, as explained at length, is spoken in the context of being free from grasping at a self, having truly entered into the Bodhisattva vehicle. If one asks why that is, it demonstrates the initial question itself: one should view the Bodhisattva who is abiding beyond the limit of realization as understanding the distinctiveness of the self, saying, "I am abiding in that." By practicing in that way, "I shall thus firmly hold the mind." The statement "Now I shall cause sentient beings to attain complete nirvāṇa," and so forth, is the elaboration.

Regarding that, the statement "Subhūti, I cognize the immeasurable and even more immeasurable eons," and so forth, as explained at length, indicates that which is supreme. This is the arising of the heap of merit of this [sūtra], and that heap of merit is supreme and surpasses all others. Regarding that, it should be understood that for as long as the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara existed, it was for immeasurable eons; the statement that "by that, one has pleased [the Buddhas] in ways that are even more immeasurable" is a summary. "Not having produced a thought" means being without pride.

heading: མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་དུས་སུ་བདག་གོ་སྙམ་དུ་འཛིན་པས་དབེན་པ།
translation: As an antidote to that, there is abiding in that, and also how one should abide, how one should practice, and how one should firmly hold the mind.

[2-92] translation already produced for this document:
The statement "How," and so forth, as explained at length, is spoken in the context of being free from grasping at a self, having truly entered into the Bodhisattva vehicle. If one asks why that is, it demonstrates the initial question itself: one should view the Bodhisattva who is abiding beyond the limit of realization as understanding the distinctiveness of the self, saying, "I am abiding in that." By practicing in that way, "I shall thus firmly hold the mind." The statement "Now I shall cause sentient beings to attain complete nirvāṇa," and so forth, is the elaboration.

As an antidote to that, there is abiding in that, and also how one should abide, how one should practice, and how one should firmly hold the mind.

heading: མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་དུས་སུ་བདག་གོ་སྙམ་དུ་འཛིན་པས་དབེན་པ།
translation: The statement, "Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva engages in the perception of a sentient being," is intended to mean that this arises from grasping at correctness or from latent tendencies. The statement, "Abiding in the vehicle of the Bodhisattva of perfect, complete enlightenment," is spoken as an antidote to grasping at a self.

Therefore, because there is no phenomenon that is actually obtained, he attained perfect and complete buddhahood beyond that limit; thus, it should be understood that the intention here is the statement, "Therefore, I was predicted."

The statement, "Abiding in the vehicle of the Bodhisattva of perfect, complete enlightenment," is spoken as an antidote to grasping at a self.

[2-96] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཐེག་པ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཞུགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་དེ་གང་ཡང་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བས་ཀྱང་ངོ་། །

heading: གདམས་ངག་ཡོངས་སུ་འཚོལ་བ།
translation: Why is it said that there is no phenomenon that is actually obtained? Subhūti, it is said that what is called a Tathāgata is the true suchness. Regarding that, the synonym for suchness is the Tathāgata, who is distinguished by perfect purity; the intention is that suchness itself is also not obtained. Regarding the expression of perfectly pure suchness and true suchness, the "true" is like gold.

heading: གདམས་ངག་ཡོངས་སུ་འཚོལ་བ།
translation: In order to abandon the grasping that "I have not fully awakened to any phenomenon from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, but I, the Blessed One, have fully awakened later," he speaks at length, saying, "Subhūti, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment..."

heading: གདམས་ངག་ཡོངས་སུ་འཚོལ་བ།
translation: Subhūti, the statement that "the phenomena to which the Tathāgata has perfectly awakened are neither true nor false" clearly demonstrates the non-duality of suchness. How is it not true? It is because there is nothing to be obtained. How is it not false? It is because of the way in which perfect and complete buddhahood is attained; for in that, there is no occurrence of anything being actually obtained.

heading: གདམས་ངག་ཡོངས་སུ་འཚོལ་བ།
translation: Therefore, what is the intention behind the Tathāgata’s statement that "all phenomena are the qualities of a buddha"? source: མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས། རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ་དཔེར་ན་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཞིག་མིའི་ལུས་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་ལུས་ཆེན་པོར་གྱུར་ཞེས་རྒྱ་ཆེར་གསུངས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། འདིས་ནི་མངོན་པར་རྟོག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཐོབ་པ་དང་། མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་མེད་པ་གསལ་བར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཅི་ལྟར་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཐོབ་པས་ཤེ་ན། ཡེ་ཤེས་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཉེ་བར་བཟུང་ནས་ཏེ། རིགས་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དང་། མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་སོ། །ཡེ་ཤེས་གང་ཞིག་ཐོབ་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་རིགས་སུ་སྐྱེས་པ་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་སུ་རིགས་ངེས་པར་གྱུར་པ་སྟེ། དེ་ནི་རིགས་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཡིན་ལ། དེ་ཐོབ་པས་ནི་ལུས་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །འདིས་ནི་གང་དུ་ཚེ་རབས་མང་པོར་མངོན་པར་དགའ་བར་བྱེད་པ་སྟེ། རིགས་སུ་སྐྱེས་པར་གྱུར་པ་དེ་ནི་ལུས་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེའི་ཕྱིར་ལུས་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པར་བྱའོ། །མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱང་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་རྣམ་པ་ལྔ་ཉེ་བར་བཟུང་ནས་ཏེ། གནས་ངན་ལེན་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་དང་། བདག་མེད་པ་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་དང་། སྤོང་བ་ལ་བརྩོན་པ་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་དང་།ཟང་ཟིང་མེད་པའི་སེམས་ལ་བརྩོན་པ་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་དང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པ་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་དོ། །དེ་དག་ཐོས་པས་ལུས་ཆེན་པོར་གྱུར་པ་སྟེ། སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་ལུས་ཉེ་བར་ལེན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེའི་ལུས་དེ་ནི་རང་གི་མ་ཡིན་ཞིང་གཞན་གྱི་མ་ཡིན་ལ་གནས་པར་ནུས་པའོ། །
translation: In terms of realization, the statement, "Subhūti, it is as if a person were endowed with a human body and had become a great body," is explained extensively. This clearly demonstrates the attainment of the gnosis of realization and the absence of the pride of realization. How is the gnosis attained? It is by taking up two types of gnosis: the gnosis that fully grasps the lineage and the gnosis of equality. The gnosis by which one is born into the lineage of the Tathāgata, becoming definitively established in the lineage of a buddha, is the gnosis that fully grasps the lineage; by attaining this, one becomes endowed with a body. This refers to that which causes one to rejoice for many lifetimes; one who has been born into the lineage becomes endowed with a body, and therefore it is called "endowed with a body." The gnosis of equality is also taken up by way of five types of equality: the equality of the latent propensity for defilement, the equality of selflessness, the equality of diligence in abandonment, the equality of diligence in a mind free from attachment, and the equality of the realization of all bodhisattvas. By hearing these, one becomes a "great body," because one takes up the bodies of all sentient beings. That body of his is neither his own nor another's, yet he is able to abide in it.

[2-104] translation already produced for this document:
Because of the ultimate establishment that "all phenomena are not established as phenomena," it is said, "Subhūti, what are called 'all phenomena' are all devoid of phenomena; therefore, they are called 'the qualities of a buddha.'"

heading: མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པ།
translation: Therefore, the statement by the Tathāgata, "a person endowed with a human body and a great body," is explained extensively by the Tathāgata as "not having a body," and so on. Regarding this, "endowed with a body" and "great body" establish the mode of ultimate reality here, which is, for the time being, through the attainment of gnosis.

It is by taking up two types of gnosis: the gnosis that fully grasps the lineage and the gnosis of equality. The gnosis by which one is born into the lineage of the Tathāgata, becoming definitively established in the lineage of a buddha, is the gnosis that fully grasps the lineage; by attaining this, one becomes endowed with a body. This refers to that which causes one to rejoice for many lifetimes; one who has been born into the lineage becomes endowed with a body, and therefore it is called "endowed with a body." The gnosis of equality is also taken up by way of five types of equality: the equality of the latent propensity for defilement, the equality of selflessness, the equality of diligence in abandonment, the equality of diligence in a mind free from attachment, and the equality of the realization of all bodhisattvas. By hearing these, one becomes a "great body," because one takes up the bodies of all sentient beings. That body of his is neither his own nor another's, yet he is able to abide in it.

heading: ཞིང་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: "Subhūti, any bodhisattva who has the conviction that 'phenomena are selfless, phenomena are selfless'" is stated with regard to the two types of selflessness: the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena. The statement, "The Tathāgata calls them a 'bodhisattva', a 'bodhisattva'," is made with regard to the two types of perfect awakening to those very two types of selflessness. If one asks what this clarifies, it is that the grasping at a person as "I shall accomplish" and the grasping at phenomena as "the arrays of the buddha-kṣetra" do not exist in those bodhisattvas.

heading: བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་མཐོང་བ་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
source: བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་མཐོང་བ་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས། རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཇི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་ཤའི་སྤྱན་མངའ་སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་རྒྱ་ཆེར་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ནི་གཟིགས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་ཕུལ་དུ་བྱུང་བ་མངའ་བ་ཉིད་དུ་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་ཁོ་ན་མངའ་བ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། སྤྱན་རྣམ་པ་ལྔ་མངའ་བ་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །གཞན་དུ་ན་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་ཁོ་ནས་གཟིགས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་ཚོལ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ལ་བསྡུས་ན་སྤྱན་རྣམ་པ་བཞི་སྟེ། གཟུགས་འཛིན་པར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། དོན་དམ་པའི་བདེན་པ་འཛིན་པར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། །ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཀྱི་བདེན་པ་འཛིན་པར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཤེས་བྱ་ཐམས་ཅད་འཛིན་པར་བྱེད་པའོ། །གཟུགས་འཛིན་པར་བྱེད་པ་ཡང་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཏེ།ལས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་དང་། བསྒོམས་པའི་འབྲས་བུའོ། །དེས་ན་རྣམ་པ་ལྔར་འགྱུར་རོ། །རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའི་ཡུལ་ཅན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་གཟུགས་འཛིན་པ་ནི་དང་པོའོ། །དོན་དམ་པ་མཁྱེན་པའི་དབང་གིས་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ལ་མཁྱེན་པ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འཇུག་སྟེ། དེའི་ཕྱིར་དོན་དམ་པའི་བདེན་པ་འཛིན་པ་སྔ་མའོ། །དེ་ལ་ཆོས་དང་གང་ཟག་ཏུ་མངོན་པར་བརྗོད་པ་ནི་ཆོས་དང་གང་ཟག་ཏུ་བཏགས་པའོ། །དེ་དག་མཁྱེན་པ་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། འདི་ནི་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་གཟིགས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པའོ། །
translation: Based on the perfection of unsurpassed vision and primordial wisdom, it is stated at length: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye?" In order to make it known that the Tathāgata possesses supreme and perfectly pure vision, it is shown that he does not possess only the eye of prajñāpāramitā, but that he possesses the five types of eyes. Otherwise, one would seek perfectly pure vision only through the eye of prajñāpāramitā. In summary, there are four types of eyes: the one that perceives form, the one that perceives the ultimate truth, the one that perceives conventional truth, and the one that perceives all knowable things in every aspect. The one that perceives form is also of two types: the result of karma and the result of meditation. Therefore, there are five types. The first is the perception of form due to having a vast object. Because of knowing the ultimate, one engages in knowing the conventional without error; therefore, the perception of the ultimate truth is the former. Regarding that, what is expressed as phenomena and persons is what is designated as phenomena and persons. Knowing those is called the eye of Dharma; this is the perfectly pure vision of the extent of all things.

རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་འདི་སྐད་དུ། ཆོས་རྣམས་ནི་བདག་མེད་པ་ཆོས་རྣམས་ནི་བདག་མེད་པའོ་ཞེས་མོས་པ་ཞེས་པ་ནི་བདག་མེད་པ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས་གསུངས་པ་སྟེ། གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་པ་དང་ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་མེད་པའོ། །དེ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ་ཞེས་པ་ནི་བདག་མེད་པ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་པོ་དེ་ཉིད་རྫོགས་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་པ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས་གསུངས་པ་སྟེ། འདིས་ཅི་ཞིག་གསལ་བར་བྱས་ཤེ་ན། གང་ཞིག་བདག་གིས་བསྒྲུབ་པོ་ཞེས་གང་ཟག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པ་དང་། ཞིང་བཀོད་པ་རྣམས་ཞེས་ཆོས་སུ་འཛིན་པ་སྟེ།དེ་དག་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ལ་མེད་ཅེས་པའོ། །
[2-111] translation already produced for this document:
"Subhūti, any bodhisattva who has the conviction that 'phenomena are selfless, phenomena are selfless'" is stated with regard to the two types of selflessness: the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena. The statement, "The Tathāgata calls them a 'bodhisattva', a 'bodhisattva'," is made with regard to the two types of perfect awakening to those very two types of selflessness. If one asks what this clarifies, it is that the grasping at a person as "I shall accomplish" and the grasping at phenomena as "the arrays of the buddha-kṣetra" do not exist in those bodhisattvas.

heading: བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་མཐོང་བ་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: The statement, "I fully know the continuum of minds of those various beings with their diverse intentions," refers to perfectly pure primordial wisdom. Regarding that, the continuum of minds refers to the minds of the three times. Regarding that, diverse intentions should be understood as being of two types: afflicted and purified, or what is called "with attachment" and "without attachment," and so forth. Alternatively, it is by the division of past and so forth.

བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་མཐོང་བ་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས། རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཇི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་ཤའི་སྤྱན་མངའ་སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་རྒྱ་ཆེར་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ནི་གཟིགས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་ཕུལ་དུ་བྱུང་བ་མངའ་བ་ཉིད་དུ་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་ཁོ་ན་མངའ་བ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། སྤྱན་རྣམ་པ་ལྔ་མངའ་བ་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་སྟོན་ཏོ། །གཞན་དུ་ན་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་ཁོ་ནས་གཟིགས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་ཚོལ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ལ་བསྡུས་ན་སྤྱན་རྣམ་པ་བཞི་སྟེ། གཟུགས་འཛིན་པར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། དོན་དམ་པའི་བདེན་པ་འཛིན་པར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། །ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཀྱི་བདེན་པ་འཛིན་པར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཤེས་བྱ་ཐམས་ཅད་འཛིན་པར་བྱེད་པའོ། །གཟུགས་འཛིན་པར་བྱེད་པ་ཡང་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཏེ།ལས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་དང་། བསྒོམས་པའི་འབྲས་བུའོ། །དེས་ན་རྣམ་པ་ལྔར་འགྱུར་རོ། །རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའི་ཡུལ་ཅན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་གཟུགས་འཛིན་པ་ནི་དང་པོའོ། །དོན་དམ་པ་མཁྱེན་པའི་དབང་གིས་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ལ་མཁྱེན་པ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་འཇུག་སྟེ། དེའི་ཕྱིར་དོན་དམ་པའི་བདེན་པ་འཛིན་པ་སྔ་མའོ། །དེ་ལ་ཆོས་དང་གང་ཟག་ཏུ་མངོན་པར་བརྗོད་པ་ནི་ཆོས་དང་གང་ཟག་ཏུ་བཏགས་པའོ། །དེ་དག་མཁྱེན་པ་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། འདི་ནི་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་གཟིགས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པའོ། །
[2-112] translation already produced for this document:
Based on the perfection of unsurpassed vision and primordial wisdom, it is stated at length: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye?" In order to make it known that the Tathāgata possesses supreme and perfectly pure vision, it is shown that he does not possess only the eye of prajñāpāramitā, but that he possesses the five types of eyes. Otherwise, one would seek perfectly pure vision only through the eye of prajñāpāramitā. In summary, there are four types of eyes: the one that perceives form, the one that perceives the ultimate truth, the one that perceives conventional truth, and the one that perceives all knowable things in every aspect. The one that perceives form is also of two types: the result of karma and the result of meditation. Therefore, there are five types. The first is the perception of form due to having a vast object. Because of knowing the ultimate, one engages in knowing the conventional without error; therefore, the perception of the ultimate truth is the former. Regarding that, what is expressed as phenomena and persons is what is designated as phenomena and persons. Knowing those is called the eye of Dharma; this is the perfectly pure vision of the extent of all things.

heading: བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་མཐོང་བ་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: In this way, both are established in terms of ultimate reality; the statement "the continuum of mind is no continuum" and the statement "the past mind is also not to be apprehended" are taught extensively. Regarding that, the past mind is not to be apprehended because it has subsided. The future mind is not to be apprehended because it has not arisen. The present mind is ultimate reality, and it is established as a vision based upon the nature of the object of knowledge that is directly perceived. Then, there is the primordial wisdom that is based upon teaching the intentions of sentient beings just as they are; this is what is meant by the statement, "Here, the continuum of mind is no continuum." If one asks why it was not similarly stated, "Regarding the perfectly pure vision, the eye is no eye," it is because the primordial wisdom and the perfectly pure vision are a single basis, and because what is established as the ultimate, final reality is established from the very beginning.

[2-113] translation already produced for this document:
The statement, "I fully know the continuum of minds of those various beings with their diverse intentions," refers to perfectly pure primordial wisdom. Regarding that, the continuum of minds refers to the minds of the three times. Regarding that, diverse intentions should be understood as being of two types: afflicted and purified, or what is called "with attachment" and "without attachment," and so forth. Alternatively, it is by the division of past and so forth.

In this way, both are established in terms of ultimate reality; the statement "the continuum of mind is no continuum" and the statement "the past mind is also not to be apprehended" are taught extensively. Regarding that, the past mind is not to be apprehended because it has subsided. The future mind is not to be apprehended because it has not arisen. The present mind is ultimate reality, and it is established as a vision based upon the nature of the object of knowledge that is directly perceived. Then, there is the primordial wisdom that is based upon teaching the intentions of sentient beings just as they are; this is what is meant by the statement, "Here, the continuum of mind is no continuum." If one asks why it was not similarly stated, "Regarding the perfectly pure vision, the eye is no eye," it is because the primordial wisdom and the perfectly pure vision are a single basis, and because what is established as the ultimate, final reality is established from the very beginning.

Having focused on the perfection of the mind and the attainment of complete awakening, it is taught extensively, "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata think that there is any Dharma whatsoever by which he has attained the unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening?" Having completely abandoned the fault of the view that "there is no such Dharma," one seeks out awakening and the path to awakening; this is taught by means of two awakenings and two definitive expressions. This is by taking up the expression "unsurpassed" and the expression "perfectly," for the statement *anuttarāyāṃ samyaksambodhau dharmā na vidyante* takes up the expression *anuttarā* to reveal the own-nature of awakening. For that awakening, which has the nature of liberation, there is not even an atom of a conditioned phenomenon that arises; for that very reason, it is not an object of apprehension. By that very fact, one should know that in the "subsequent" "Dharma" "existence," there is no existence.

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Revealing awakening from the general characteristic of the phenomena of cyclic existence, it is said: "By all wholesome phenomena, one is fully awakened." Revealing the path of awakening in its entirety, it is said: "Those are just so; those too are established by the characteristic of ultimate reality."

[2-122] source:
ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར། ས་མཿས་དྷརྨཿ ཞེས་པས་ནི་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སྒྲ་ཉེ་བར་བཟུང་ནས་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལས་གང་ཟག་སྤྱིའི་མཚན་ཉིད་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་དེ། དེ་ལ་ཆོས་དེ་ནི་མཉམ་པ་སྟེ་ཞེས་པ་ནི་ཆོས་གང་གིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་སུ་གདགས་པའོ། །
[2-122] translation already produced for this document:
Furthermore, Subhūti, by the phrase *samāḥ sa dharmāḥ*, the expression "perfectly complete" is taken up to reveal the general characteristic of the person in relation to awakening; the statement "that Dharma is equal" refers to that by which one is designated as awakening and as a Buddha.

[2-123] source:
དེ་ལ་མི་མཉམ་པ་གང་ཡང་མེད་པས་ཤེས་པས་ནི། སངས་རྒྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་དོན་དམ་པར་སྐུ་ཚེ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡང་མི་མཉམ་པ་མེད་པར་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །
[2-123] translation already produced for this document:
By knowing that there is nothing whatsoever that is unequal in that regard, it is shown that all Buddhas, in the ultimate sense, are also without inequality regarding their life span and so forth.

[2-124] source:
བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་དེ་ནི་སྲོག་མེད་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་མཉམ་པའོ་ཞེས་སོ། །
[2-124] translation already produced for this document:
It is said that that unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening is equal by virtue of being without a life-principle.

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: What is the intention behind the statement that the Tathāgata would be grasping at a self? It should be viewed as follows: if the Tathāgata were to conceive of sentient beings because he knows the knowable exactly as it is, then the Tathāgata would be grasping at a self.

[2-125] translation already produced for this document:
Revealing awakening from the general characteristic of the phenomena of cyclic existence, it is said: "By all wholesome phenomena, one is fully awakened." Revealing the path of awakening in its entirety, it is said: "Those are just so; those too are established by the characteristic of ultimate reality."

[2-126] source:
ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དོན་ཆེན་པོ་རྣམ་པར་གཞག་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས། སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སྟོང་ཆེན་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་ན་རི་རབ་ཇི་སྙེད་ཡོད་པ་ཞེས་རྒྱ་ཆེར་གསུངས་སོ། །
[2-126] translation already produced for this document:
With the intention of establishing the great meaning of the perfect mind, it is said extensively: "In the world system of the third-order great trichiliocosm, as many Mount Sumerus as there are," and so forth.

[2-127] source:
དོན་ཆེན་པོ་གདམས་ངག་རྣམ་པར་བཞག་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་ངས་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་བཀྲོལ་ལོ་ཞེས་དགོངས་སོ་སྙམ་ན་ཞེས་རྒྱ་ཆེར་གསུངས་སོ། །
[2-127] translation already produced for this document:
With the intention of establishing the great meaning of the instruction, it is said extensively: "If you think, 'The Tathāgata thinks: I have liberated sentient beings,'" and so forth.

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: In order to abandon the intense attachment of thinking that, although there is no self, there is for the time being a grasping at a self, it is said extensively: "Subhūti, the so-called 'grasping at a self' is a non-grasping."

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: The statement that although childish ordinary beings grasp at it as existing, it does not exist to be grasped, is explained extensively by the phrase: "Subhūti, the so-called 'childish ordinary beings' are those who are not beings," and those are just so.

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: With regard to the perfect excellence of the mind, which is the Dharmakāya, it is said extensively: "Subhūti, what do you think? Should the Tathāgata be viewed by means of the perfect excellence of marks?" The first verse clearly demonstrates how one does not see and by whom one does not see. If one asks how one does not see, it is by means of conventions such as "view." What is called "abandoning" is meditative absorption; whoever is a practitioner of meditative absorption is called one who abandons, and that consists of both reflection and cultivation. Through reflection, one grasps at what is not that, and through cultivation, one cognizes incorrectly; it should be understood that by engaging in abandoning, one grasps at the convention of incorrect cognition. If one asks by whom one does not see, it is by those beings who are engaged in conventions.

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Regarding the cause by which one knows, it is said: "The Guides are the Dharmakāya." Because the Buddhas, who are all-pervading and focused on suchness, are the pure body, they should be viewed as Dharmatā; this is how one views them. If one asks again, by what cause are they not to be viewed? Because the Dharmatā, which is the characteristic of suchness, cannot be cognized by literal interpretation, and because it must be realized by each individual for themselves, it is said that one cannot cognize it through non-literal interpretation either, as one does not see it. The statement that clearly demonstrates this meaning is: "Since Dharmatā cannot be cognized, it cannot be cognized by that." Similarly, here, the fact that the basis of the Dharmakāya is not to be viewed as the Tathāgata is demonstrated by the statement "not by the perfect excellence of marks," meaning that the perfect excellence of marks is not to be viewed as the Tathāgata.

With regard to the perfect excellence of the mind, which is the Dharmakāya, it is said extensively: "Subhūti, what do you think? Should the Tathāgata be viewed by means of the perfect excellence of marks?" The first verse clearly demonstrates how one does not see and by whom one does not see. If one asks how one does not see, it is by means of conventions such as "view." What is called "abandoning" is meditative absorption; whoever is a practitioner of meditative absorption is called one who abandons, and that consists of both reflection and cultivation. Through reflection, one grasps at what is not that, and through cultivation, one cognizes incorrectly; it should be understood that by engaging in abandoning, one grasps at the convention of incorrect cognition. If one asks by whom one does not see, it is by those beings who are engaged in conventions.

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Then, in order to not abide in nirvāṇa and to completely abandon the association with the defilements of cyclic existence, it is stated at length: "Again, Subhūti, a son or daughter of noble family..." Regarding the meaning of "those phenomena that are selfless and unborn," what is it? That which the Tathāgata has mastered, whose engagement is of the nature of an emanation, is not the nature of the phenomena of cyclic existence, nor does it arise from karma and defilements; that which has become subject to one's control is called "selfless and unborn." What is the reason for understanding this? Otherwise, if one were not to become defiled in cyclic existence by merely holding onto the merit as described, then what need is there to mention bodhisattvas who have patience in the selfless and unborn? For by attaining patience in the unborn, an immense amount of merit will arise.

Then, in order to not abide in nirvāṇa and to completely abandon the association with the defilements of cyclic existence, it is stated at length: "Again, Subhūti, a son or daughter of noble family..." Regarding the meaning of "those phenomena that are selfless and unborn," what is it? That which the Tathāgata has mastered, whose engagement is of the nature of an emanation, is not the nature of the phenomena of cyclic existence, nor does it arise from karma and defilements; that which has become subject to one's control is called "selfless and unborn." What is the reason for understanding this? Otherwise, if one were not to become defiled in cyclic existence by merely holding onto the merit as described, then what need is there to mention bodhisattvas who have patience in the selfless and unborn? For by attaining patience in the unborn, an immense amount of merit will arise.

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: The Venerable Subhūti asked, "What is the intention behind the statement 'one should not grasp at a mass of merit'? For the Bhagavan has elsewhere stated that one should grasp at a mass of merit."

translation: The Bhagavan replied, "Although one should grasp at it, one should not grasp at it wrongly; thus, by way of this distinction, it is taught that it should be grasped. How one should not grasp at it wrongly is just as previously explained; it is those very points."

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: With regard to the physical postures of movement and abiding, which are the perfection of the mind, it is stated at length: "Again, Subhūti, if someone were to say, 'The Tathāgata comes or goes...'" In this context, movement refers to walking, and abiding refers to standing. The remainder refers to the physical postures.

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: "Bhagavan, if there were a world-system, it would be an apprehension of a whole"—this statement was spoken by taking as the object both what the world-system is and what an atom is. Apprehension of a whole is of two types: apprehension of a whole as a unity, and apprehension of a whole by way of analysis. Regarding these, the existence of a world-system is an apprehension of a whole as a unity, such as thinking "a sentient being" in relation to the aggregates; and the existence of an atom is an apprehension of a whole by way of analysis, for it is an apprehension of a whole by grasping at a collection of atoms.

It is said that what is grasped by ordinary childish beings is merely according to worldly convention, and not in the ultimate sense. Having explained the meditation on the method for making appearances non-existent, [the text] also establishes the yoga and meditative equipoise that make appearances non-existent; and that which is called "non-conceptualizing" is precisely non-conceptualizing as it is.

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: How is this so? The assertion of a self by other, non-Buddhist schools, and the Tathāgata’s speaking of a self, are both established as the selflessness of the person. That the view of a self is also spoken of as having no view establishes the selflessness of phenomena. If one engages in such a practice—where there is no apprehension of a view regarding that view of a self—one will enter into meditative equipoise; thus, that non-conceptualization is the method for entering into it.

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: Subhūti, the phrase "entering correctly into the vehicle of the Bodhisattva" fully demonstrates who it is that engages in non-conceptualization. The phrase "all phenomena" indicates that upon which one is to engage in non-conceptualization. The phrase "should be known, should be seen, should be resolved upon" begins from the higher mind and higher wisdom; by means of knowing, seeing, and resolving, it indicates by what means one is to engage in non-conceptualization. In this regard, that which relies on śamatha is prajñā. That which relies on vipaśyanā is jñāna. Both seeing and knowing are here the samādhi of resolution, and by the power of samādhi, one resolves intensely upon the object as if it were a reflection.

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: The phrase "one should resolve in such a way that one does not abide even in the perception of phenomena" fully demonstrates what the conceptualization is, and those are precisely it. The "perception of phenomena" indicates the meaning of the logic of the uncommon; this is the method for entering into meditative equipoise, and it should be understood as the basis for everything. One should engage only to the extent of cutting off aspiration, prayer, and distraction. Therefore, the method has been explained by those points, and it is exactly like that.

[2-150] translation already produced for this document:
Subhūti, the phrase "entering correctly into the vehicle of the Bodhisattva" fully demonstrates who it is that engages in non-conceptualization. The phrase "all phenomena" indicates that upon which one is to engage in non-conceptualization. The phrase "should be known, should be seen, should be resolved upon" begins from the higher mind and higher wisdom; by means of knowing, seeing, and resolving, it indicates by what means one is to engage in non-conceptualization. In this regard, that which relies on śamatha is prajñā. That which relies on vipaśyanā is jñāna. Both seeing and knowing are here the samādhi of resolution, and by the power of samādhi, one resolves intensely upon the object as if it were a reflection.

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: In order to demonstrate the perfection of the mind, and having taken as the basis the absence of defilement, it is further stated at length: "Subhūti, by what means does a bodhisattva mahāsattva..." What does this demonstrate? Because this Dharma possesses great meaning, it must undoubtedly be clarified correctly. Nevertheless, it must be clarified in such a way that it does not become a source of defilement.

[2-150] translation already produced for this document:
Subhūti, the phrase "entering correctly into the vehicle of the Bodhisattva" fully demonstrates who it is that engages in non-conceptualization. The phrase "all phenomena" indicates that upon which one is to engage in non-conceptualization. The phrase "should be known, should be seen, should be resolved upon" begins from the higher mind and higher wisdom; by means of knowing, seeing, and resolving, it indicates by what means one is to engage in non-conceptualization. In this regard, that which relies on śamatha is prajñā. That which relies on vipaśyanā is jñāna. Both seeing and knowing are here the samādhi of resolution, and by the power of samādhi, one resolves intensely upon the object as if it were a reflection.

heading: ཐུགས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ།
translation: What is the intention behind saying, "How does one correctly demonstrate? It is by demonstrating in such a way that one does not demonstrate at all; therefore, it is called correctly demonstrating"? It means that the Dharma, which is of the nature of being inexpressible, cannot be demonstrated. Otherwise, it would be demonstrated through affliction, and because that meaning is erroneous, there is no supreme clarity or aspiration toward such a demonstration. Therefore, the Dharma is demonstrated without affliction, and that is exactly how it is.

source: ཨེ་ཏཱ་ད་ཤཱི་མརྠ་ག་ཏིཾ་ནི་ཤཱ་མྱ། ཡེ་ཥཱཾ་མ་ཧཱ་ཡཱ་ན་མ་བདྡྷཽ་མེ་བ། ཏཱ་ནསྨནོ་བེདྨི་ན་བཱསྨ་ནོ་པི། གུ་ཎཻ་ར་བྷཱ་བྱཱ་ནླ་སུ་ནཱ་ན་བཻ་མི། ཧཱི་ནོ་ཧི་གཱམྦྷཱིཪྻ་མུ་དཱ་ར་ཏཱམྦཱ། བོདྡྷུནྣ་ཤཀྣཱ་ཏི་ན་ཙཱ་དྷི། མོཀྟུཾ། པྲཱ་ཡེ་ཎ་ཙོཾ་བཾ་བི་དྷ་ཨེ་ཥ་ལོ་ཀཿ ཏེ་ནཱ་ཏྲ་དྷརྨེ་ཁི་ལ་ཏཱམྤྲ་ཡཱ་ཏཿ འཕགས་པ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་མ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་གཅོད་པའི་གནས་བདུན་གྱི་རྒྱ་ཆེར་འགྲེལ་པ། སློབ་དཔོན་དབྱིག་གཉེན་གྱིས་མཛད་པ་རྫོགས་སོ།། །།ཞེས་པ་འདི་ནི་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་གཞོན་ནུ་དཔལ་བའི་ཞལ་སྔ་ནས་གསར་འགྱུར་མཛད་པའི་འཕྲོ་ཅུང་ཟད་ལུས་པ། རྗེ་དམ་པ་དེའི་དགོངས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པའི་སླད་དུ་འགྱུར་བར་གྱིས་ཤིག་ཅེས། ཞྭ་དམར་ཅོད་པན་འཛིན་པ་བཞི་པ། དཔལ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་གྲགས་པ་ཡེ་ཤེས་དཔལ་བཟང་པོའི་ཞལ་སྔ་ནས་བཀའ་སྩལ་བ་སྤྱི་བོས་མནོས་ཏེ། ཞ་ལུ་ལོ་ཙཱ་བ་འགོས་ཆོས་སྐྱོང་བཟང་པོས། ལུགས་གཉིས་ཀྱི་མདུན་ས་ཆེན་པོ་ཕོ་བྲང་སྣེའུ་གདོང་རྩེར། ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྗེ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་པོ་ཆེན་པོ་དཔལ་ངག་གི་དབང་ཕྱུག་གྲགས་པ་ཕྱོགས་ཐམས་ཅད་ལས་རྣམ་པར་རྒྱལ་བའི་དཔལ་གྱི་མངའ་ཐང་ཆེན་པོ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ལེགས་པར་བསྒྱུར་བའོ། །དུས་གསུམ་རྒྱལ་བ་སྐྱེད་མ་རྡོ་རྗེའི་མཚན་ཅན་ཟབ་མོའི་དགོངས་འགྲེལ་རབ་གསལ་བ། །ཀུན་མཁྱེན་གཉིས་པ་དབྱིག་གཉེན་ཞེས་གྲགས་དཔལ་ལྡན་ཤིང་རྟ་ཆེན་པོས་རྣམ་པར་བཀོད། །གང་དེ་ཁ་བ་ཅན་པའི་དཔལ་དུ་གཞོན་ནུའི་མཚན་ཅན་མཁས་གྲུབ་མཆོག་གིས་བསྒྱུར། །དེ་ཉིད་རྫོགས་པར་བསྒྱུར་བའི་དགེ་བས་འདྲེན་པ་མཆོག་དེའི་དགོངས་པ་རྫོགས་གྱུར་ཅིག །སླར་ཡང་རྒྱ་དཔེ་ལ་གཏུགས་ཤིང་སློབ་དཔོན་ཀ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལས་མཛད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པར་བརྗོད་བྱ་རིས་མཐུན་པ་རྣམས་དང་སྦྱར་ཏེ་ཚིག་ཕྲད་དང་འཁྲུགས་སྡེབ་པ་སོགས་ཅུང་ཟད་ལེགས་ཆར་འགྱུར་བ་རྣམས་འབད་ཅིང་དག་པར་བགྱིས་སོ།། །།
translation: [The Sanskrit verses are omitted here as they are a corrupted transliteration of the preceding Tibetan text.] The Extensive Commentary on the Seven Points of the Noble Bhagavatī Mother Prajñāpāramitā Vajracchedikā, composed by the master Vasubandhu, is complete. This text was left slightly unfinished by the omniscient Zhonnu Pal, and at the request of the fourth holder of the red crown, the glorious Chökyi Drakpa Yeshe Pal Sangpo, who commanded that it be completed so that the intention of that holy master might be fully realized, I, the Zhalu translator Gö Chökyong Sangpo, have accepted this command upon my head. It was well translated at the great seat of the two systems, the palace of Nêdong Tsé, relying upon the great power and sovereignty of the Lord of Dharma, the great Dharma-king, the glorious Ngakgi Wangchuk Drakpa, who is victorious in all directions. The profound commentary, which clarifies the meaning of the Vajracchedikā, the mother of the victors of the three times, was set forth by the second omniscient one, the glorious and great chariot, the master Vasubandhu. It was translated by the supreme scholar and adept, the one bearing the name of youth, for the glory of the Land of Snows. May the merit of completing this translation fulfill the intention of that supreme guide. Furthermore, by comparing it with the Sanskrit manuscript and aligning it with the corresponding subject matter in the commentary composed by the master Kamalaśīla, I have exerted myself to correct and refine the text, including the particles and the arrangement of the phrasing, to make it slightly better.

སེམས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་སྟོན་པ་ལ་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས། ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་གང་གིས་ཞེས་རྒྱ་ཆེར་གསུངས་སོ། །འདིས་ཅི་ཞིག་བསྟན་ཞེ་ན། ཆོས་འདི་དོན་ཆེན་པོ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གདོན་མི་ཟ་བར་ཡང་དག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་གསལ་བར་བྱ་བའོ། །དེ་ལྟ་མོད་ཀྱི་ཅི་ནས་ཀྱང་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་ལྟར་རབ་ཏུ་གསལ་བར་བྱ་བའོ། །
[2-152] translation already produced for this document:
In order to demonstrate the perfection of the mind, and having taken as the basis the absence of defilement, it is further stated at length: "Subhūti, by what means does a bodhisattva mahāsattva..." What does this demonstrate? Because this Dharma possesses great meaning, it must undoubtedly be clarified correctly. Nevertheless, it must be clarified in such a way that it does not become a source of defilement.

[2-153] source:
ཅི་ལྟར་ཡང་དག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་ཞེ་ན། ཅི་ནས་ཀྱང་རབ་ཏུ་མི་སྟོན་པ་བཞིན་དུ་སྟེ། དས་ན་ཡང་དག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ་ཞེས་པའི་དགོངས་པ་ཅི་ཞེ་ན། བརྗོད་དུ་མེད་པར་བསྟན་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ནི་བསྟན་པར་བྱར་མེད་པ་སྟེ། གཞན་དུ་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པས་བསྟན་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དོན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་པ་ལ་ལྷག་པར་དང་བ་དང་དོན་དུ་གཉེར་བ་མེད་དོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པར་ཆོས་བསྟན་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ་དེ་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་ནོ། །
[2-153] translation already produced for this document:
What is the intention behind saying, "How does one correctly demonstrate? It is by demonstrating in such a way that one does not demonstrate at all; therefore, it is called correctly demonstrating"? It means that the Dharma, which is of the nature of being inexpressible, cannot be demonstrated. Otherwise, it would be demonstrated through affliction, and because that meaning is erroneous, there is no supreme clarity or aspiration toward such a demonstration. Therefore, the Dharma is demonstrated without affliction, and that is exactly how it is.

[2-154] source:
སེམས་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་འཁོར་བར་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ནས། སྐར་མ་རབ་རིབ་མར་མེ་དང་། ཞེས་པའི་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པ་སྟེ། དོན་ནི་སྔར་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་ཏེ་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ། །

Having taken as the basis the perfection of the mind and the absence of affliction in samsāra, the verse beginning with "stars, optical aberration, a butter lamp..." is stated; the meaning is as it was previously, and it has already been explained.

source: ཨེ་ཏཱ་ད་ཤཱི་མརྠ་ག་ཏིཾ་ནི་ཤཱ་མྱ། ཡེ་ཥཱཾ་མ་ཧཱ་ཡཱ་ན་མ་བདྡྷཽ་མེ་བ། ཏཱ་ནསྨནོ་བེདྨི་ན་བཱསྨ་ནོ་པི། གུ་ཎཻ་ར་བྷཱ་བྱཱ་ནླ་སུ་ནཱ་ན་བཻ་མི། ཧཱི་ནོ་ཧི་གཱམྦྷཱིཪྻ་མུ་དཱ་ར་ཏཱམྦཱ། བོདྡྷུནྣ་ཤཀྣཱ་ཏི་ན་ཙཱ་དྷི། མོཀྟུཾ། པྲཱ་ཡེ་ཎ་ཙོཾ་བཾ་བི་དྷ་ཨེ་ཥ་ལོ་ཀཿ ཏེ་ནཱ་ཏྲ་དྷརྨེ་ཁི་ལ་ཏཱམྤྲ་ཡཱ་ཏཿ འཕགས་པ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་མ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་གཅོད་པའི་གནས་བདུན་གྱི་རྒྱ་ཆེར་འགྲེལ་པ། སློབ་དཔོན་དབྱིག་གཉེན་གྱིས་མཛད་པ་རྫོགས་སོ།། །།ཞེས་པ་འདི་ནི་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་གཞོན་ནུ་དཔལ་བའི་ཞལ་སྔ་ནས་གསར་འགྱུར་མཛད་པའི་འཕྲོ་ཅུང་ཟད་ལུས་པ། རྗེ་དམ་པ་དེའི་དགོངས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པའི་སླད་དུ་འགྱུར་བར་གྱིས་ཤིག་ཅེས། ཞྭ་དམར་ཅོད་པན་འཛིན་པ་བཞི་པ། དཔལ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་གྲགས་པ་ཡེ་ཤེས་དཔལ་བཟང་པོའི་ཞལ་སྔ་ནས་བཀའ་སྩལ་བ་སྤྱི་བོས་མནོས་ཏེ། ཞ་ལུ་ལོ་ཙཱ་བ་འགོས་ཆོས་སྐྱོང་བཟང་པོས། ལུགས་གཉིས་ཀྱི་མདུན་ས་ཆེན་པོ་ཕོ་བྲང་སྣེའུ་གདོང་རྩེར། ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྗེ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་པོ་ཆེན་པོ་དཔལ་ངག་གི་དབང་ཕྱུག་གྲགས་པ་ཕྱོགས་ཐམས་ཅད་ལས་རྣམ་པར་རྒྱལ་བའི་དཔལ་གྱི་མངའ་ཐང་ཆེན་པོ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ལེགས་པར་བསྒྱུར་བའོ། །དུས་གསུམ་རྒྱལ་བ་སྐྱེད་མ་རྡོ་རྗེའི་མཚན་ཅན་ཟབ་མོའི་དགོངས་འགྲེལ་རབ་གསལ་བ། །ཀུན་མཁྱེན་གཉིས་པ་དབྱིག་གཉེན་ཞེས་གྲགས་དཔལ་ལྡན་ཤིང་རྟ་ཆེན་པོས་རྣམ་པར་བཀོད། །གང་དེ་ཁ་བ་ཅན་པའི་དཔལ་དུ་གཞོན་ནུའི་མཚན་ཅན་མཁས་གྲུབ་མཆོག་གིས་བསྒྱུར། །དེ་ཉིད་རྫོགས་པར་བསྒྱུར་བའི་དགེ་བས་འདྲེན་པ་མཆོག་དེའི་དགོངས་པ་རྫོགས་གྱུར་ཅིག །སླར་ཡང་རྒྱ་དཔེ་ལ་གཏུགས་ཤིང་སློབ་དཔོན་ཀ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལས་མཛད་པའི་འགྲེལ་པར་བརྗོད་བྱ་རིས་མཐུན་པ་རྣམས་དང་སྦྱར་ཏེ་ཚིག་ཕྲད་དང་འཁྲུགས་སྡེབ་པ་སོགས་ཅུང་ཟད་ལེགས་ཆར་འགྱུར་བ་རྣམས་འབད་ཅིང་དག་པར་བགྱིས་སོ།། །།
translation:
etādṛśīm arthagatīṃ niśāmya yeṣāṃ mahāyānam abuddham eva |
tān asmabhedīna vā smanopī guṇair abhāvyān na sunānabhaimi ||
hīnā hi gāmbhīryam udāratāṃ vā boddhuṃ na śaknanti na cādhimoktum |
prāyeṇa cāyaṃ vidha eṣa lokaḥ tenātra dharme khilatāṃ prayātaḥ ||

The Extensive Commentary on the Seven Points of the Noble Bhagavatī Mother Prajñāpāramitā Vajracchedikā, composed by the master Vasubandhu, is complete.

This text is the continuation of the new translation begun by the omniscient Zhonnu Pal. In order to fully complete the intention of that holy lord, the fourth holder of the red crown, the glorious Chökyi Drakpa Yeshe Pal Sangpo, gave the command, which I received upon my head. Thus, I, the Zhalu translator Gö Chökyong Zangpo, have translated it well, relying upon the great seat of the two systems at the palace of Nêdong Tsé, and the great power and glory of the lord of Dharma, the great Dharma-king, the glorious Ngakgi Wangchuk Drakpa, who is victorious in all directions.

The profound commentary, which clarifies the meaning of the Vajracchedikā, the mother of the victors of the three times, was set forth by the second omniscient one, the great glorious chariot, known as Vasubandhu. It was translated by the supreme scholar and adept, the one bearing the name of youth, for the glory of the Land of Snows. May the merit of completing this translation fulfill the intention of that supreme guide.

Furthermore, I have exerted myself to correct and refine the text by consulting the Sanskrit original and aligning it with the corresponding subject matter in the commentary composed by the master Kamalaśīla, thereby improving the phrasing and the arrangement of the text.

[2-152] translation already produced for this document:
In order to demonstrate the perfection of the mind, and having taken as the basis the absence of defilement, it is further stated at length: "Subhūti, by what means does a bodhisattva mahāsattva..." What does this demonstrate? Because this Dharma possesses great meaning, it must undoubtedly be clarified correctly. Nevertheless, it must be clarified in such a way that it does not become a source of defilement.

ཅི་ལྟར་ཡང་དག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་ཞེ་ན། ཅི་ནས་ཀྱང་རབ་ཏུ་མི་སྟོན་པ་བཞིན་དུ་སྟེ། དས་ན་ཡང་དག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ་ཞེས་པའི་དགོངས་པ་ཅི་ཞེ་ན། བརྗོད་དུ་མེད་པར་བསྟན་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ནི་བསྟན་པར་བྱར་མེད་པ་སྟེ། གཞན་དུ་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པས་བསྟན་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དོན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་པ་ལ་ལྷག་པར་དང་བ་དང་དོན་དུ་གཉེར་བ་མེད་དོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པར་ཆོས་བསྟན་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ་དེ་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་ནོ། །
[2-153] translation already produced for this document:
What is the intention behind saying, "How does one correctly demonstrate? It is by demonstrating in such a way that one does not demonstrate at all; therefore, it is called correctly demonstrating"? It means that the Dharma, which is of the nature of being inexpressible, cannot be demonstrated. Otherwise, it would be demonstrated through affliction, and because that meaning is erroneous, there is no supreme clarity or aspiration toward such a demonstration. Therefore, the Dharma is demonstrated without affliction, and that is exactly how it is.
